exam: A 45‑year‑old diabetic woman presents with early satiety and vomiting of undigested food; what test confirms the diagnosis and what threshold is diagnostic? — Gastric emptying scintigraphy; >60 % retention at 2 h.

You suspect colonic inertia in a patient with chronic constipation; which bedside test helps differentiate functional from obstructive causes? — Digital rectal examination for empty rectum and absence of palpable mass; supports functional delay.
A patient on long‑term antipsychotics develops severe constipation; which medication should be avoided and why? — Anticholinergics; they further reduce gut motility.
In a low‑resource hospital without manometry, how would you assess esophageal dysmotility? — Barium swallow looking for delayed transit and lack of peristalsis; correlate with symptoms.
Why is erythromycin not recommended for chronic use in motility disorders? — Risk of bacterial resistance and QT prolongation.

A patient with HIV presents with abdominal distension; stool PCR is positive for TB. How does TB cause dysmotility and what is the primary treatment? — TB induces granulomatous inflammation of the myenteric plexus; treat with standard anti‑TB regimen.
What red‑flag symptom mandates immediate admission in a patient with suspected gastroparesis? — Persistent vomiting with electrolyte imbalance or metabolic alkalosis.
How would you counsel a patient with mild gastroparesis on diet? — Small, low‑fat, low‑fiber meals every 2–3 hours; avoid lying down after eating.
ai.title: Gastrointestinal Motility Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Disorders of coordinated gut movement cause symptoms from dysphagia to chronic constipation. Diagnosis relies on history, bedside tests and selective investigations, with management focused on underlying cause and symptom control.

b: Absence of a structural blockage on imaging
Reproducible abnormal motility on manometry or scintigraphy
sections.p: Abnormal propulsion or coordination of the gastrointestinal tract without mechanical obstruction, confirmed by clinical criteria and functional tests.

b: Mild: intermittent symptoms, normal weight
Moderate: daily symptoms, weight loss <10 %
Severe: refractory symptoms, weight loss ≥10 % or dependence on tube feeding
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden, nutritional status and need for parenteral support.

b: Diabetes mellitus (autonomic neuropathy)
Chronic HIV infection or antiretroviral toxicity
Tuberculosis affecting the gut wall or nerves
Schistosomiasis‑related fibrosis
Post‑surgical vagal injury
Herbal remedies causing smooth‑muscle inhibition
sections.p: Etiologies are grouped into neurogenic, myogenic, metabolic and secondary to infection or drugs, with tropical infections high on the list in low‑resource settings.

b: Gastroparesis: post‑prandial fullness, vomiting of undigested food
Esophageal dysmotility: dysphagia, chest pain, regurgitation
Colonic inertia: >3 days constipation, palpable fecal mass
sections.p: Presentation varies with the affected segment; upper GI dysmotility gives early satiety, nausea and vomiting, while distal disease causes constipation, abdominal distension and pain.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical pattern, response to empirical pro‑kinetic therapy and basic labs.

t.b: Excludes mechanical obstruction; normal lumen suggests functional cause
Answers whether gastric emptying is delayed; >60 % retention at 2 h confirms gastroparesis
Assesses peristaltic amplitude and coordination; absent peristalsis points to achalasia‑like disorder
Determines segmental delay; >70 % markers retained at 72 h indicates colonic inertia
Identifies metabolic contributors; abnormal values guide targeted therapy

t.a: Stool ova and parasites, TB PCR on stool
t.b: Detects tropical infections when motility is secondary to inflammation

b: Weight loss ≥10 % in 3 months
Persistent vomiting with metabolic alkalosis
Signs of intestinal ischemia (sudden severe pain, peritonitis)
sections.p: Uncontrolled vomiting, severe malnutrition, electrolyte disturbance and bacterial overgrowth can be life‑threatening.

b: Correct hyperglycaemia in diabetic patients – improves autonomic function
Metoclopramide (dopamine antagonist) for gastroparesis; avoid in patients with Parkinson’s or seizure risk
Erythromycin (macrolide) as motilin agonist; limited to short courses to prevent resistance
Domperidone where available – less CNS penetration, monitor QTc
Avoid anticholinergics and opioids as they worsen motility
Enteral feeding via jejunostomy or parenteral nutrition for severe cases
sections.p: Treat reversible causes, optimise nutrition and use pro‑kinetic agents judiciously.

b: Monthly weight and symptom diary
Quarterly HbA1c for diabetic patients
Review need for pro‑kinetics every 3 months
sections.p: Regular review of weight, glycaemic control and medication side‑effects; educate patients on small‑frequent meals and avoidance of offending drugs.

b: Irritable bowel syndrome – pain improves with defecation, no motility test abnormality
Mechanical obstruction – visible transition point on plain X‑ray or CT
sections.p: Functional bowel disorders and mechanical obstruction share symptoms but differ in imaging and response to pro‑kinetics.

b: Normal gastric emptying study in early disease – repeat if symptoms persist
Electrolyte shifts may mask underlying metabolic cause
sections.p: Normal imaging does not exclude dysmotility; early diabetic gastroparesis may have borderline scintigraphy.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs
